Interview-Driven discovery runs structured workshops with the people who own a journey end to end — product managers, channel owners, customer-facing teams — to walk through every step where personal data is captured, including offline and human-mediated touchpoints a technical scan cannot see, such as a call-centre script or a paper KYC form later digitised.
Scan-Driven discovery works from the artefacts a system leaves behind: front-end source code, form and API definitions, third-party SDK call sites, and application logs, surfacing collection points directly from what is actually deployed rather than from what stakeholders remember or believe is deployed. It is particularly effective at catching collection points added by past teams, acquired products, or third-party embeds that no current employee is aware of.
In practice we run both in every CDJR build engagement, in either order depending on client maturity: Scan-Driven discovery first when a client's documentation is thin and code is the more reliable source of truth, Interview-Driven first when the priority is capturing offline touchpoints and organisational context that no scan will ever surface. The two tracks are reconciled against each other before any collection point is marked Live-ready, since discrepancies between what a scan finds and what a stakeholder describes are themselves valuable findings.


---

## Industries Hub
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/

Banking, Financial Services & Insurance: High-volume, high-sensitivity personal and financial data processing under simultaneous DPDPA and RBI/IRDAI oversight.
Healthcare & Life Sciences: Health data processing that combines DPDPA obligations with medical confidentiality norms and, frequently, Legitimate Uses exemptions for emergency care.
Education Technology: Children's data at the centre of the product, triggering the DPDPA's strictest consent category.
E-commerce & Direct-to-Consumer: High-frequency consent collection across marketing, personalisation and logistics, at consumer scale.
SaaS & IT Services: B2B and B2B2C products where the company is frequently both a Data Fiduciary for its own users and a Data Processor for enterprise customers.
Manufacturing: Lower consumer-facing exposure but significant employee, dealer and IoT sensor data footprint.
Government & Public Sector Undertakings: Unique exemption pathways under the Act alongside large-scale citizen data processing responsibilities.
Insurance: Health, financial and beneficiary data combined with actuarial profiling, under IRDAI and DPDPA oversight together.
Telecommunications: Location, call and usage data at national scale, combined with existing sector-specific regulatory obligations.
Media & Entertainment: Audience data, viewing behaviour and increasingly personalised content recommendation engines.
HR-Tech & Staffing: Candidate and employee personal data, including background checks and, increasingly, algorithmic screening tools.
Real Estate & PropTech: Buyer, tenant and financing data shared across a fragmented ecosystem of brokers, developers and lenders.
Logistics & Supply Chain: Delivery, address and contact data at extremely high transaction volume, shared across multi-party fulfilment networks.


---

## Industry: Banking, Financial Services & Insurance
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/bfsi/

High-volume, high-sensitivity personal and financial data processing under simultaneous DPDPA and RBI/IRDAI oversight.

Risks: KYC and financial data qualify as high-sensitivity personal data requiring rigorous security safeguards; RBI data localisation mandates for payment systems apply alongside, not instead of, the DPDPA; Large legacy core-banking and CRM systems often predate any formal consent architecture; Cross-selling between group entities (banking, credit cards, mutual funds) raises Purpose Limitation questions; High rights-request volume expected once Data Principal awareness grows


---

## Industry: Healthcare & Life Sciences
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/healthcare-life-sciences/

Health data processing that combines DPDPA obligations with medical confidentiality norms and, frequently, Legitimate Uses exemptions for emergency care.

Risks: Health records are highly sensitive even though DPDPA does not use a separate "sensitive data" category; Deemed Consent and Legitimate Uses provisions for medical emergencies must be applied narrowly and correctly; Hospital networks and diagnostic chains often share data across legal entities without clear Data Processor agreements; Research and clinical trial data raises complex secondary-purpose and consent-scope questions; Patient rights requests (access, correction) intersect with medical record retention obligations under other laws


---

## Industry: Education Technology
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/edtech/

Children's data at the centre of the product, triggering the DPDPA's strictest consent category.

Risks: Verifiable Parental Consent is required wherever a child's personal data is processed; Behavioural tracking and targeted advertising to children face specific restrictions; Age-verification mechanisms are often weak or entirely absent in growth-stage EdTech products; School and institutional data-sharing arrangements frequently lack proper Data Processor terms; Rapid feature shipping cycles routinely outpace privacy review


---

## Industry: E-commerce & Direct-to-Consumer
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/ecommerce-d2c/

High-frequency consent collection across marketing, personalisation and logistics, at consumer scale.

Risks: Marketing consent is frequently bundled with account creation, failing the specificity standard; Third-party ad-tech and analytics SDKs create collection points product teams may not be aware of; Logistics partners handling name, address and phone number require proper Data Processor agreements; High-volume rights requests during sale periods can overwhelm ad hoc fulfilment processes; Retargeting and personalisation profiling needs explicit purpose disclosure


---

## Industry: SaaS & IT Services
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/saas-it/

B2B and B2B2C products where the company is frequently both a Data Fiduciary for its own users and a Data Processor for enterprise customers.

Risks: Dual role as Data Fiduciary and Data Processor requires clear contractual and operational separation; Enterprise customers increasingly require DPDPA compliance evidence in security questionnaires; Multi-tenant architectures complicate per-customer data segregation and deletion; Cross-border engineering and support teams raise data-access and localisation questions; Sub-processor chains (cloud infra, monitoring, analytics tools) need systematic due diligence


---

## Industry: Manufacturing
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/manufacturing/

Lower consumer-facing exposure but significant employee, dealer and IoT sensor data footprint.

Risks: Employee personal data (biometric attendance, payroll, health records) is often under-governed; Dealer and distributor personal data is frequently exchanged without formal agreements; IoT and factory-floor sensor data increasingly intersects with personal data where operators are identifiable; Legacy ERP and HR systems predate any DPDPA-aligned retention discipline; Vendor and contractor access to personal data is rarely audited


---

## Industry: Government & Public Sector Undertakings
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/government-psu/

Unique exemption pathways under the Act alongside large-scale citizen data processing responsibilities.

Risks: Certain government functions may qualify for specific exemptions, but scope must be assessed precisely, not assumed broadly; Citizen-scale data holdings carry outsized breach and misuse consequences; Interoperability with other government databases raises purpose-limitation and consent questions; Legacy systems built long before any privacy-by-design discipline existed; Public accountability and RTI obligations intersect with data protection duties in ways that need careful navigation


---

## Industry: Insurance
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/insurance/

Health, financial and beneficiary data combined with actuarial profiling, under IRDAI and DPDPA oversight together.

Risks: Underwriting profiling requires clear purpose disclosure and proportionality justification; Claims investigation data-sharing with third parties (hospitals, garages, assessors) needs formal Data Processor terms; Nomination and beneficiary data intersects directly with the DPDPA's own Nomination right; Agent networks handling personal data at point of sale are a common unmanaged risk; Legacy policy records often lack a documented consent trail


---

## Industry: Telecommunications
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/telecom/

Location, call and usage data at national scale, combined with existing sector-specific regulatory obligations.

Risks: Call detail records and location data are highly sensitive and heavily used for secondary analytics; Existing telecom-specific regulations must be reconciled with DPDPA obligations rather than treated as a substitute; Partner and reseller networks create extended data-sharing chains; SIM registration and KYC processes are high-volume collection points needing consistent consent architecture; Law-enforcement and lawful-interception obligations intersect with, but do not eliminate, DPDPA duties for other processing


---

## Industry: Media & Entertainment
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/media-entertainment/

Audience data, viewing behaviour and increasingly personalised content recommendation engines.

Risks: Viewing and engagement profiling for recommendations requires clear purpose disclosure; Advertising partnerships and data-sharing arrangements are frequently under-contracted; Children's content platforms carry the same Verifiable Parental Consent obligations as EdTech; User-generated content platforms face unique data-minimisation and moderation-data questions; Cross-platform identity resolution (web, app, connected TV) fragments consent state


---

## Industry: HR-Tech & Staffing
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/hrtech-staffing/

Candidate and employee personal data, including background checks and, increasingly, algorithmic screening tools.

Risks: Background verification checks process highly sensitive personal data through third-party vendors; Algorithmic resume screening and candidate scoring tools need fairness and accuracy review; Candidate data retention after a hiring decision is frequently indefinite and undocumented; Client (employer) and candidate data flows create a three-party consent and disclosure structure; Cross-border staffing arrangements raise transfer questions for candidate data


---

## Industry: Real Estate & PropTech
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/real-estate-proptech/

Buyer, tenant and financing data shared across a fragmented ecosystem of brokers, developers and lenders.

Risks: Lead-generation forms often collect financial and identity data with minimal notice; Broker and channel-partner networks share personal data with no formal agreements; Site-visit and biometric access-control systems in gated communities process personal data with little governance; Financing and loan-referral partnerships intersect with BFSI-grade sensitivity without BFSI-grade controls; Long sales cycles mean stale lead data accumulates without a retention policy


---

## Industry: Logistics & Supply Chain
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/industries/logistics/

Delivery, address and contact data at extremely high transaction volume, shared across multi-party fulfilment networks.

Risks: Delivery partner apps and gig-worker platforms process personal data with inconsistent governance; Address and contact data is shared across a chain of fulfilment partners, warehouses and last-mile riders; Real-time location tracking of delivery personnel intersects with employee/gig-worker privacy expectations; High transaction volume makes rights-request fulfilment at scale a genuine operational challenge; E-commerce platform integrations create collection points logistics teams may not directly control


---

## Glossary Hub
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/

Adjudicating Officer: The Data Protection Board member or officer empowered to conduct inquiries and impose penalties under the DPDPA.
Anonymization: The process of rendering personal data no longer identifiable to a specific individual, taking it outside the Act's scope — if done rigorously.
Appellate Tribunal: The forum for appeals against Data Protection Board orders — the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT) under the DPDPA framework.
Automated Decision-Making: Decisions made about a Data Principal through automated processing, without meaningful human involvement — an area of growing regulatory attention.
Automated Means: Any equipment capable of automatically operating in response to instructions given for performing specific tasks — the technical basis of the Act's "processing" scope.
Breach Notification Timeline: The window within which a Data Fiduciary must notify the Data Protection Board and affected Data Principals of a personal data breach.
Central Consent Engine: A rule-based service architecture that enforces the consent and purpose rules defined in a Digital Personal Data Register (DPDR) and Customer Data Journey Registry (CDJR) at runtime.
Child's Data: Personal data of an individual under 18, subject to the DPDPA's strictest consent and processing restrictions.
Collection Point: The specific touchpoint — a form, screen, script, or API — where personal data is originally captured from a Data Principal.
Consent Artefact: The structured, machine-readable record of a specific consent event — what was consented to, when, under which notice version, and how.
Consent Fatigue: The degraded quality of consent decisions that results from Data Principals being asked to consent too frequently, too vaguely, or too repetitively.
Consent Manager: A registered entity that lets Data Principals give, manage, review and withdraw consent across multiple Data Fiduciaries through one interface.
Consent Manager Registration: The process and criteria by which an entity becomes a registered Consent Manager with the Data Protection Board.
Consent Withdrawal Propagation: The technical and operational process of ensuring a consent withdrawal actually stops downstream processing across every system that received the data.
Cross-Border Data Transfer: Transfer of personal data outside India — permitted by default under the DPDPA, subject to any government-notified restrictions.
Data Audit: A periodic, independent review of a Data Fiduciary's data processing activities and compliance posture, required of Significant Data Fiduciaries.
Data Breach: Any unauthorised processing, or accidental disclosure, acquisition, sharing, or loss of access, of personal data that compromises its confidentiality, integrity or availability.
Data Element: A single, discrete field of personal data — such as an email address or PAN — and the base unit of granularity in a structured data register.
Data Fiduciary: Any person who alone or with others determines the purpose and means of processing personal data — the primary duty-bearer under the DPDPA.
Data Fiduciary Accuracy Obligation: The duty to ensure personal data used to make a decision affecting a Data Principal, or disclosed to another Fiduciary, is accurate and complete.
Data Fiduciary Contact Person: The individual or department a Data Principal can contact regarding their personal data, required of every Data Fiduciary.
Data Fiduciary Contact Publication: The requirement that Data Fiduciaries make contact details for data protection queries readily and prominently available to Data Principals.
Data Fiduciary Obligations: The umbrella set of duties the DPDPA imposes on every Data Fiduciary — notice, consent, security, accuracy, retention, and rights fulfilment.
Data Localisation: A requirement that certain data be stored or processed within a specific country's borders, distinct from and layered on top of DPDPA transfer rules.
Data Minimization: Collecting and retaining only the personal data genuinely necessary for the disclosed purpose — no more, "just in case."
Data Principal: The individual to whom the personal data relates — the person the DPDPA is designed to protect.
Data Principal Rights (DPR): The umbrella term for the full set of rights the DPDPA grants individuals over their own personal data — access, correction, erasure, grievance redressal, nomination and withdrawal.
Data Processor: An entity that processes personal data on behalf of a Data Fiduciary, under the Fiduciary's instructions.
Data Protection Board: The regulatory and adjudicatory body established under the DPDPA to enforce the Act, primarily operating digitally.
Data Protection by Design: The practice of embedding privacy considerations into product and system design from the earliest stage, rather than retrofitting compliance after launch.
Data Protection Impact Assessment: A structured evaluation of the necessity, proportionality and risk of a specific processing activity, mandatory for Significant Data Fiduciaries.
Data Protection Officer: The individual designated to represent a Data Fiduciary's data protection function — mandatory for Significant Data Fiduciaries.
Data Retention: The obligation to erase personal data once its purpose is fulfilled and retention is no longer necessary for a legal or business reason.
Data Sharing Disclosure: The obligation to disclose, as part of the right to access, the identities of Data Processors and other Data Fiduciaries a Data Principal's data has been shared with.
Deemed Consent: An earlier drafting-era term now generally absorbed into the DPDPA's "Legitimate Uses" provisions covering consent-free processing scenarios.
Digital Personal Data: The DPDPA's actual scope: personal data in digital form, and personal data collected offline that is later digitised.
Draft DPDP Rules, 2025: The subordinate legislation that operationalises the DPDPA 2023's framework provisions with specific procedural detail.
Employment Purposes: A recognised Legitimate Use allowing processing of employee personal data necessary for employment-related purposes without separate consent for each instance.
Exemptions: Specific categories of processing or entities the DPDPA exempts, wholly or partly, from particular provisions of the Act.
Grievance Redressal Officer: The individual responsible for responding to a Data Principal's grievance regarding the processing of their personal data.
Harm: A broadly defined concept under the DPDPA covering bodily, psychological, financial, reputational and other injury a Data Principal may suffer from data misuse.
Independent Data Auditor: A third-party auditor who conducts the periodic data audit required of Significant Data Fiduciaries, distinct from internal compliance review.
Instrumentality of State: A related concept to State Instrumentality, describing bodies substantially controlled by government that may fall within specific DPDPA exemption provisions.
Legitimate Uses: Specific scenarios under the DPDPA where personal data may be processed without obtaining consent, distinct from Deemed Consent.
Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY): The administering ministry responsible for the DPDPA's implementation, Rules-making, and the constitution of the Data Protection Board.
Notice: The disclosure a Data Fiduciary must give a Data Principal before or at the time of seeking consent, in clear and plain language.
Notice Language Requirements: The DPDPA requires notice content be available, at the Data Principal's option, in English or a language listed in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution.
Penalties & Adjudication: The DPDPA's financial penalty regime, adjudicated by the Data Protection Board, with penalties reaching up to ₹250 crore for the most severe breaches.
Personal Data: Any data about an individual who is identifiable by or in relation to that data — the DPDPA's foundational scope term.
Processing: Any wholly or partly automated operation performed on digital personal data — collection, storage, use, sharing, disclosure, erasure, and more.
Profiling: Automated processing used to analyse or predict aspects of a Data Principal's behaviour, preferences or attributes.
Public Interest Processing: Processing carried out for functions like providing benefits, subsidies, licences, or services, which the Act treats through specific Legitimate Use and exemption provisions.
Purpose: The specific, disclosed reason personal data is collected or processed — the unit of granularity the DPDPA's notice and consent requirements are built around.
Purpose Limitation: The principle that personal data may only be processed for the specific purpose disclosed and consented to — not repurposed silently.
Purpose Taxonomy: A defined, non-overlapping list of processing purposes an organisation uses consistently across notices, consent flows, and data registers.
Reasonable Security Safeguards: The obligation to protect personal data through appropriate technical and organisational measures proportionate to risk.
Research, Archiving and Statistical Purposes Exemption: A specific exemption for processing carried out for research, archiving, or statistical purposes, subject to standards the Central Government may prescribe.
Right of Nomination: A Data Principal's right to nominate another individual to exercise their rights in the event of death or incapacity.
Right to Access: A Data Principal's right to obtain a summary of their personal data being processed and the processing activities undertaken.
Right to Correction and Erasure: A Data Principal's right to have inaccurate or incomplete personal data corrected, and to have data erased once no longer necessary.
Right to Grievance Redressal: A Data Principal's right to have a readily available means of registering a grievance about processing or rights fulfilment.
Rights Fulfilment SLA: The internally defined target turnaround time for responding to a specific type of Data Principal rights request.
Sensitive Personal Data: A nuanced concept: the DPDPA itself does not formally define a separate "sensitive" category, unlike GDPR or India's earlier SPDI Rules.
Significant Data Fiduciary: A Data Fiduciary designated by the Central Government for enhanced obligations, based on factors like data volume, sensitivity and risk.
State Instrumentality: A concept relevant to how certain exemptions and obligations apply differently to government bodies and their instrumentalities under the Act.
Verifiable Parental Consent: The heightened consent standard required before processing a child's personal data — consent must be genuinely verifiable, not merely self-declared.
Voluntary Undertaking: A commitment a Data Fiduciary can voluntarily offer to the Data Protection Board to address a compliance issue, potentially resolving proceedings without a full penalty order.
Withdrawal of Consent: A Data Principal's right to withdraw previously given consent at any time, with a withdrawal process as easy to use as the consent process.


---

## Glossary: Data Fiduciary
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-fiduciary/

A Data Fiduciary is the entity — company, individual, or organisation — that decides why personal data is being processed and how. It is the DPDPA's equivalent of a "data controller" in other privacy regimes, and it carries the primary compliance burden: giving notice, obtaining valid consent, implementing reasonable security safeguards, and honouring Data Principal rights. Almost every organisation that collects customer, employee, or user data is a Data Fiduciary for at least some of that data, even if it also acts as a Data Processor for other data it merely processes on someone else's instructions. Determining fiduciary status precisely — and where the lines blur in outsourced or platform-based models — is often the first analytical step in a Gap Assessment.


---

## Glossary: Data Principal
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-principal/

The Data Principal is the natural person whose personal data is being collected or processed. Where a child's data is involved, the Act treats the parent or lawful guardian as exercising rights on the child's behalf; for a person with a disability who has a lawful guardian, the guardian similarly acts on their behalf. Every obligation in the Act — notice, consent, security, rights fulfilment — exists to protect the Data Principal's interest in their own personal data, which is why "who is the Data Principal here, and are we treating them accordingly" is a useful sanity check to run against any new product feature or data flow.


---

## Glossary: Data Processor
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-processor/

A Data Processor handles personal data strictly on the instructions of, and on behalf of, a Data Fiduciary — a cloud hosting provider, a payroll processing vendor, a customer-support BPO. The Data Fiduciary remains accountable for that processing even though it isn't performing it directly, which is why Data Processing Agreements matter: they are the contractual mechanism that binds the Processor to the Fiduciary's instructions and to relevant DPDPA obligations like breach notification and deletion on termination. Many organisations occupy both roles simultaneously for different data sets — a SaaS company is typically a Fiduciary for its own employee and marketing data, and a Processor for the customer data its enterprise clients store in its platform.


---

## Glossary: Significant Data Fiduciary
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/significant-data-fiduciary/

The Central Government may designate any Data Fiduciary, or class of Data Fiduciaries, as a Significant Data Fiduciary (SDF) based on criteria including the volume and sensitivity of personal data processed, risk of harm to Data Principals, potential impact on India's sovereignty and integrity, risk to electoral democracy, security of the state, and public order. SDFs carry an enhanced compliance tier: appointing a India-based DPO reporting to the board, appointing an independent data auditor, conducting periodic DPIAs and data audits, and evaluating the algorithmic systems they use for processing. We help organisations assess SDF designation exposure before it becomes a formal notification.


---

## Glossary: Consent Manager
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/consent-manager/

A Consent Manager is a person registered with the Data Protection Board that acts as a single point through which a Data Principal can grant, manage, and withdraw consent across multiple Data Fiduciaries, accountable to the Data Principal. It is a novel intermediary category not found in most other privacy regimes, intended to reduce "consent fatigue" from having to manage separate consent relationships with every organisation a person interacts with. Consent Managers must meet technical, financial and operational registration criteria set by the Board. Using a Consent Manager is not currently mandatory for most Data Fiduciaries, but designing your own consent architecture to be interoperable with the model is sound forward planning as the ecosystem matures.


---

## Glossary: Data Protection Board
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-protection-board/

The Data Protection Board of India (DPB) is the body established to enforce the DPDPA — receiving breach notifications, inquiring into complaints and non-compliance, issuing directions, and imposing penalties through its adjudicatory function. It is designed to operate as a digital-first office, meaning most proceedings are expected to happen online rather than through traditional in-person hearings. Unlike a conventional court, the Board's remit is specifically the Act's obligations — it does not replace sector regulators like RBI or IRDAI, whose rules continue to apply independently and in parallel.


---

## Glossary: Data Protection Officer
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-protection-officer/

A Data Protection Officer (DPO) is the senior individual who owns an organisation's data protection governance — chairing privacy reviews, owning grievance redressal, advising on new products, and representing the organisation to the Data Protection Board if needed. Significant Data Fiduciaries must appoint a DPO based in India who reports directly to the board or an equivalent governing body. Other Data Fiduciaries must designate a contact person for Data Principal queries even without a full DPO appointment. Our DPO-as-a-Service offering provides fractional, senior DPO coverage for organisations not yet ready to make a full-time hire.


---

## Glossary: Data Fiduciary Contact Person
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-fiduciary-contact-person/

Every Data Fiduciary must publish the contact details of a person or department able to answer Data Principal questions about the processing of their personal data, even where a full Data Protection Officer has not been appointed. In practice this is often the first, most visible compliance artefact a Data Principal — or a regulator — will look for, since its absence signals that even basic accountability infrastructure has not been established. We treat setting this up correctly as a same-week fix in almost every Gap Assessment.


---

## Glossary: Personal Data
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/personal-data/

Personal data is any data about an individual who is identifiable by or in relation to such data. The definition is deliberately broad and identifiability-based, rather than built around a fixed list of "personal identifiers" — meaning data that seems anonymous in isolation can still be personal data if it is reasonably re-identifiable when combined with other information the organisation holds or can access. The Act applies specifically to digital personal data, and to personal data collected in non-digital form that is subsequently digitised — a distinction worth getting precisely right when scoping what falls inside your compliance perimeter.


---

## Glossary: Sensitive Personal Data
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/sensitive-personal-data/

This is one of the more misunderstood points in DPDPA compliance conversations. Unlike the EU GDPR (with its "special categories") or India's earlier IT Rules SPDI framework (which listed specific sensitive categories like health and financial data), the DPDPA 2023 does not create a separate statutory tier of "sensitive personal data" with distinct handling rules. Every category of personal data is, in principle, subject to the same core obligations. In practice, however, data that would be considered sensitive elsewhere — health records, financial details, biometric data, children's data — still warrants materially higher operational caution, because the harm from mishandling it is greater and because sector regulators (RBI, IRDAI, healthcare bodies) often impose their own heightened handling requirements independently of the DPDPA. We advise clients to keep a practical risk-based sensitivity tiering internally, even though the Act does not formally require one.


---

## Glossary: Processing
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/processing/

Processing is defined expansively under the DPDPA to cover a wholly or partly automated operation, or set of operations, performed on digital personal data — including collection, recording, organisation, structuring, storage, adaptation, retrieval, use, alignment, combination, indexing, sharing, disclosure by transmission, dissemination, restriction, erasure or destruction. Practically, this means almost every interaction your systems have with a piece of personal data — from the moment a form is submitted to the moment a record is finally deleted — falls within scope, which is why a DPDR-style element-level inventory is the only reliable way to track it comprehensively.


---

## Glossary: Profiling
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/profiling/

Profiling refers to any form of processing of personal data that analyses or predicts aspects concerning the behaviour, attributes or interests of a Data Principal. Recommendation engines, credit scoring models, targeted advertising segmentation and fraud-risk models are all common forms of profiling. The DPDPA does not prohibit profiling outright, but it does require that profiling be disclosed as a distinct, specific purpose at the point of consent — bundling it silently into a general "improve our services" purpose is a common gap we flag during assessments, particularly for algorithmic systems Significant Data Fiduciaries are required to evaluate.


---

## Glossary: Anonymization
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/anonymization/

Anonymization removes or transforms identifying elements from a dataset so that a specific individual can no longer reasonably be identified from it, whether directly or by combination with other reasonably available information. Genuinely anonymised data falls outside the DPDPA's scope, which makes anonymization an attractive route for analytics and research use cases. The operative word is "reasonably" — poorly executed anonymization (removing a name but leaving a unique combination of postcode, birthdate and gender, for example) can still leave data re-identifiable, and re-identifiable data is still personal data regardless of what label is applied to it. We test anonymization claims rather than accepting them during Gap Assessments.


---

## Glossary: Data Breach
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-breach/

A personal data breach under the DPDPA covers unauthorised processing of personal data, or accidental or unauthorised disclosure, acquisition, sharing, use, alteration, destruction or loss of access to personal data that compromises its confidentiality, integrity or availability. This is broader than the popular notion of a "hack" — accidental disclosure, misconfiguration, or an internal access failure can all qualify. A breach triggers notification obligations to the Data Protection Board and to affected Data Principals; our Breach Response & Notification Readiness service builds the classification framework organisations need to make that call quickly and correctly when an incident actually occurs.


---

## Glossary: Cross-Border Data Transfer
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/cross-border-data-transfer/

The DPDPA takes a permissive default approach to cross-border data transfer: a Data Fiduciary may transfer personal data outside India unless the Central Government has specifically restricted transfer to that country or territory by notification. This is a materially different model from the EU GDPR's adequacy-first approach, where transfer is restricted by default absent a positive adequacy finding. Sector-specific data localisation rules — such as RBI's requirements for payment system data — continue to apply independently of the DPDPA and must be satisfied separately.


---

## Glossary: Data Localisation
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-localisation/

Data localisation mandates that specified categories of data remain stored, or be mirrored, within a country's territory. The DPDPA itself does not impose a general localisation requirement — its cross-border transfer regime is restriction-based, not localisation-based. However, sectoral regulators retain independent localisation mandates, most notably the RBI's requirement that payment system data be stored only in India. Organisations in regulated sectors must satisfy both regimes simultaneously; our Cross-Border Data Transfer Advisory service maps both layers together rather than treating DPDPA compliance as sufficient on its own.


---

## Glossary: Consent Artefact
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/consent-artefact/

A Consent Artefact is the actual evidentiary record of a Data Principal's consent: timestamp, notice version shown, purpose(s) consented to, and the mechanism used to capture it. A user-facing confirmation message ("Thanks, you're all set!") is not a Consent Artefact — it is a structured, retrievable, machine-readable record that a Data Fiduciary can produce later to demonstrate what was actually agreed to, and that downstream systems can check programmatically before processing. Designing a defensible Consent Artefact schema is a core output of our Consent Management Advisory engagements.


---

## Glossary: Legitimate Uses
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/legitimate-uses/

The DPDPA lists specific Legitimate Uses where a Data Fiduciary may process personal data without consent — including where a Data Principal has voluntarily provided their data for a specified purpose and has not indicated they do not consent, for purposes related to employment, for compliance with a judgment or court order, for medical emergencies or to provide medical treatment during epidemics and public health threats, for disaster or breakdown of public order response, and for certain state functions like providing benefits or services. Each Legitimate Use has specific conditions attached, and correctly classifying whether a given processing activity genuinely qualifies — rather than over-claiming the exemption to avoid the friction of obtaining consent — is exactly the kind of judgment call our Consent Management Advisory work is built to make defensibly.


---

## Glossary: Deemed Consent
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/deemed-consent/

Earlier drafts of India's data protection legislation used the term "deemed consent" for scenarios where consent is presumed rather than explicitly obtained — medical emergencies, employment purposes, compliance with law, and similar situations. In the enacted DPDPA 2023, this concept is expressed through the specific, enumerated Legitimate Uses provisions rather than a standalone "deemed consent" clause. The substance is similar — certain processing does not require the standard consent flow — but the precise conditions attached to each Legitimate Use in the final Act are what actually govern, and those conditions should be checked directly rather than relied on from memory of earlier drafts.


---

## Glossary: Notice
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/notice/

Section 5 of the DPDPA requires that, at or before the time of requesting consent, a Data Fiduciary give the Data Principal an itemised notice describing the personal data to be collected and the purpose of processing, in clear and plain language, along with the manner in which the Data Principal may exercise their rights and lodge a complaint with the Data Protection Board. The notice must be available in English or any language listed in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution at the Data Principal's option. Bundled, vague, or legalese-heavy notices are among the most common findings in our Gap Assessments.


---

## Glossary: Withdrawal of Consent
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/withdrawal-of-consent/

The DPDPA requires that withdrawing consent be at least as easy as giving it in the first place — a standard that most legacy "email us to unsubscribe from everything" flows fail outright. Once consent is withdrawn, the Data Fiduciary must, within a reasonable time, cease processing the personal data for the withdrawn purpose unless another legal basis applies, and must cause any Data Processor to do the same. Designing this mechanism, and the downstream operational steps it triggers, is a core deliverable of our Consent Management Advisory service.


---

## Glossary: Purpose Limitation
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/purpose-limitation/

Purpose limitation means personal data collected for one disclosed purpose cannot simply be repurposed for another without fresh notice and consent (or a valid Legitimate Use). It is one of the DPDPA's foundational principles and the reason purpose-level granularity — captured, for instance, in a Purpose ID field within a structured data register — matters more than a single blanket "we use your data to provide services" disclosure. Silent purpose creep, such as using support-ticket data collected for service purposes to later build a marketing segment, is a common and serious finding.


---

## Glossary: Data Minimization
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-minimization/

Data minimisation is the discipline of collecting only what a specific, disclosed purpose genuinely requires, and not retaining it beyond that purpose's useful life. It shows up operationally in shorter sign-up forms, tighter field-level justification during product design, and defined retention or deletion triggers rather than indefinite storage "in case it's useful later." A DPIA's necessity-and-proportionality test is largely a formal check on this principle for any specific high-risk processing activity under review.


---

## Glossary: Data Retention
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-retention/

A Data Fiduciary must erase personal data once the purpose for which it was processed is no longer being served and retention is not necessary for legal compliance, unless the Data Principal withdraws consent or the purpose is no longer specified — subject to any longer retention period required by other applicable law. In practice, this requires a defined retention schedule per data category, not an indefinite default. It is one of the fields we build directly into a client's Digital Personal Data Register as Consent Expiry, so retention discipline is enforceable at the data-element level rather than left as an abstract policy statement.


---

## Glossary: Reasonable Security Safeguards
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/reasonable-security-safeguards/

The DPDPA requires every Data Fiduciary to implement reasonable security safeguards to prevent personal data breaches, and to ensure that any Data Processor engaged also implements adequate safeguards. The Act does not prescribe a fixed technical checklist — "reasonable" is calibrated to the sensitivity of the data and the risk of harm from a breach, meaning what's reasonable for a low-risk internal tool differs from what's reasonable for a system holding financial or health data at scale. This is where DPDPA compliance and conventional information-security practice converge most directly.


---

## Glossary: Grievance Redressal Officer
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/grievance-redressal-officer/

A Data Fiduciary must provide an effective mechanism for a Data Principal to register a grievance regarding the processing of their personal data or the exercise of their rights, and must respond within a specified timeframe before the Data Principal may escalate to the Data Protection Board. In practice, this role is often held by the same Data Protection Officer or contact person, but the grievance function specifically needs a documented process — intake, investigation, response, and record-keeping — that our Data Principal Rights Fulfillment Setup service is designed to stand up.


---

## Glossary: Right to Access
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/right-to-access/

A Data Principal has the right to obtain from a Data Fiduciary a summary of the personal data being processed and the processing activities undertaken with respect to that data, along with the identities of any Data Processors and Data Fiduciaries with whom the data has been shared, and a description of the personal data shared. This is broader than simply handing over a raw data export — it requires the Data Fiduciary to be able to explain what is happening to the data, not just what data exists.


---

## Glossary: Right to Correction and Erasure
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/right-to-correction-and-erasure/

A Data Principal may request correction of inaccurate or misleading personal data, completion of incomplete data, updating of data, and erasure of personal data that is no longer necessary for the purpose for which it was processed, unless retention is required by law. Fulfilling this right operationally requires knowing exactly where a given element lives across your systems — which is precisely the traceability an Asset ID and Collection Point ID in a structured data register are designed to provide.


---

## Glossary: Right to Grievance Redressal
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/right-to-grievance-redressal/

Every Data Principal has the right to have readily available means of grievance redressal in respect of any act or omission of a Data Fiduciary regarding their personal data or the exercise of their rights. A Data Fiduciary must respond to grievances within a specified period before the Data Principal can escalate the matter to the Data Protection Board — meaning a slow or absent internal grievance process doesn't just create dissatisfaction, it accelerates a Data Principal's path to a regulatory complaint.


---

## Glossary: Right of Nomination
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/right-of-nomination/

The DPDPA gives every Data Principal the right to nominate any other individual to exercise their rights in the event of death or incapacity. This is a genuinely novel right not commonly found in other global privacy frameworks, and it requires a defined operational process — most organisations have no existing workflow for "please act on behalf of a deceased or incapacitated user's account," and building one from scratch during an actual request is far riskier than designing it in advance.


---

## Glossary: Data Principal Rights (DPR)
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-principal-rights/

Data Principal Rights (DPR) is the collective term covering the right to access a summary of processing, the right to correction and erasure, the right to grievance redressal, the right of nomination, and the right to withdraw consent. Building the operational infrastructure — intake, verification, routing, SLAs — to actually fulfil these rights at scale, rather than simply acknowledging they exist on paper, is the specific focus of our Data Principal Rights Fulfillment Setup service.


---

## Glossary: Child's Data
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/childs-data/

The DPDPA defines a child as an individual who has not completed the age of eighteen years, and imposes materially stricter requirements on processing a child's personal data: verifiable parental or lawful guardian consent is required, and Data Fiduciaries are generally restricted from processing that causes detrimental effect on a child's wellbeing, and from behavioural monitoring or targeted advertising directed at children — subject to any exemptions the Central Government notifies for specific classes of Data Fiduciaries or purposes.


---

## Glossary: Verifiable Parental Consent
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/verifiable-parental-consent/

Before processing a child's personal data, a Data Fiduciary must obtain verifiable consent from the child's parent or lawful guardian. "Verifiable" is the operative word: a simple age-gate checkbox or self-declared birthdate does not meet the bar the Act clearly intends. Designing a genuinely verifiable mechanism — without creating excessive friction or collecting even more personal data in the process of verifying age — is one of the more technically and legally delicate problems in EdTech and child-directed product design, and a recurring focus of our work in that sector.


---

## Glossary: Data Protection Impact Assessment
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-protection-impact-assessment/

A Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) evaluates whether a specific processing activity is necessary and proportionate to its purpose, and assesses the risk to the rights of Data Principals, alongside measures to mitigate that risk. Significant Data Fiduciaries must undertake DPIAs periodically as part of their enhanced obligations. Even outside that mandatory context, we recommend a DPIA discipline for any organisation launching a materially new, high-risk use of personal data — new AI features and large-scale profiling being the most common triggers.


---

## Glossary: Data Audit
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-audit/

Significant Data Fiduciaries must undertake a periodic data audit, conducted by an independent data auditor, as part of their enhanced compliance obligations. This is distinct from an internal Gap Assessment: the data audit is an ongoing, statutorily anticipated obligation performed by an independent party, whereas a Gap Assessment is typically the diagnostic engagement that gets an organisation ready for — or informs the scope of — that audit programme.


---

## Glossary: Penalties & Adjudication
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/penalties-and-adjudication/

The DPDPA sets out a schedule of financial penalties the Data Protection Board can impose for specific categories of non-compliance — failure to take reasonable security safeguards to prevent a breach, failure to notify the Board or affected Data Principals of a breach, and various obligations specific to Significant Data Fiduciaries and children's data, among others. The maximum penalty for the most serious category (inadequate security safeguards resulting in a breach) is up to ₹250 crore, with other categories carrying lower but still substantial caps. Penalties are imposed by the Board following an inquiry, with an appeal route to the Appellate Tribunal.


---

## Glossary: Adjudicating Officer
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/adjudicating-officer/

Within the Data Protection Board's structure, inquiries into complaints and instances of non-compliance are conducted, and penalties determined, through its adjudicatory function. The process is intended to run largely as a digital office, with parties able to make submissions and receive determinations through online proceedings rather than exclusively in-person hearings — reflecting the Board's broader design as a digital-first regulatory body.


---

## Glossary: Appellate Tribunal
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/appellate-tribunal/

A person aggrieved by an order or direction of the Data Protection Board may appeal to the Appellate Tribunal, which the DPDPA designates as the Telecom Disputes Settlement and Appellate Tribunal (TDSAT). This gives the enforcement framework a defined judicial-style review layer above the Board's own adjudicatory decisions, distinct from ordinary civil court litigation.


---

## Glossary: Voluntary Undertaking
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/voluntary-undertaking/

The DPDPA allows a person to offer a voluntary undertaking to the Data Protection Board, committing to take (or refrain from) specific actions related to a compliance matter under inquiry. The Board may accept such an undertaking, which can pause or resolve proceedings on agreed terms. This gives organisations a cooperative path to remediate an issue and demonstrate good faith, rather than every inquiry necessarily culminating in a contested penalty order.


---

## Glossary: Exemptions
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/exemptions/

The DPDPA carves out specific exemptions — certain processing for the enforcement of legal rights or claims, processing necessary for research, archiving or statistical purposes subject to standards the Central Government may prescribe, processing by courts and tribunals for judicial functions, and processing the Central Government notifies as exempt for reasons of sovereignty, security of the state, and public order, among others. Exemptions are narrower and more conditional than they are sometimes assumed to be in practice — correctly scoping whether a specific processing activity genuinely qualifies is a common and consequential judgment call.


---

## Glossary: State Instrumentality
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/state-instrumentality/

Certain DPDPA exemptions apply specifically to the State and its instrumentalities — government departments and bodies performing sovereign, regulatory, or welfare functions — reflecting a policy choice to allow government data processing for functions like providing subsidies, benefits, licences, and services. This does not mean government processing is unconstrained; it means the specific exemption conditions attaching to state functions need to be assessed distinctly from how the Act applies to private-sector Data Fiduciaries, which is a common point of confusion in public-sector engagements.


---

## Glossary: Digital Personal Data
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/digital-personal-data/

The Act's formal title and operative scope both centre on digital personal data — personal data collected in digital form, and personal data collected in non-digital form that is subsequently digitised. This means a purely offline, never-digitised paper record technically sits outside the Act's direct scope, though in practice almost every organisation eventually digitises what it collects, bringing it within scope at that point. Getting this boundary right matters most for organisations with significant physical-paper collection processes — retail KYC forms, hospital intake sheets — that haven't yet been fully digitised.


---

## Glossary: Automated Means
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/automated-means/

The DPDPA's definition of processing centres on operations performed through automated means — equipment that can operate automatically once instructed, whether hardware or software. This ties the Act's scope specifically to digital and automated handling of personal data, as distinct from a purely manual, non-automated process, and reinforces why the Act's title and substantive focus is squarely on digital personal data rather than personal information generally.


---

## Glossary: Central Consent Engine
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/central-consent-engine/

Once a client has built a DPDR and CDJR — the structured registers of what data is held and where it is collected — the next architectural question is how those registers actually get enforced in production, rather than sitting as reference documents no system consults. A Central Consent Engine is the rule-based service pattern that answers this: it checks, at the moment a processing action is attempted, whether valid consent for the relevant Purpose ID currently exists for that Data Principal, and blocks or allows the action accordingly. Building this engine is a technical implementation workstream distinct from — and downstream of — the register-building methodology itself, which is a consulting and design exercise we lead directly.


---

## Glossary: Data Element
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-element/

A data element is the smallest meaningful unit of personal data tracked in a compliance programme — a specific field like "customer email" or "PAN number," rather than an entire table, form, or system. Tracking compliance obligations at the data-element level, rather than at the level of a whole database or product, is what allows an organisation to answer precise questions ("why do we hold this specific field, and when must it be purged") instead of only broad ones. This is the base unit our Digital Personal Data Register methodology is built around.


---

## Glossary: Collection Point
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/collection-point/

A collection point is any specific touchpoint where personal data enters an organisation's systems from a Data Principal — a website signup form, a mobile app screen, a call-centre script, a physical KYC form, a partner data feed. Every collection point should have a corresponding notice and consent mechanism appropriate to what it collects. Mapping every collection point comprehensively — including ones added informally by product teams over time — is the specific purpose of our Customer Data Journey Registry methodology.


---

## Glossary: Purpose
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/purpose/

A purpose is the specific, itemised reason personal data is being collected — "process your order," "verify your identity for KYC," "send you promotional offers" — rather than a single catch-all justification like "provide our services." The DPDPA's notice and consent framework is fundamentally purpose-centric: notice must itemise the purpose, and consent must be specific to it. Maintaining a clean, non-overlapping purpose taxonomy across an organisation is foundational to nearly every other compliance artefact, from consent UI copy to a structured data register.


---

## Glossary: Automated Decision-Making
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/automated-decision-making/

Automated decision-making refers to decisions affecting a Data Principal made through automated or algorithmic processing with little or no human involvement — credit approval models, automated fraud flags, algorithmic content moderation. While the DPDPA does not yet impose the kind of explicit automated-decision-making rights found in GDPR, Significant Data Fiduciaries' obligation to evaluate the algorithmic systems they use for processing brings this squarely into scope for larger organisations, and it is an area we expect regulatory attention to sharpen as the Rules mature.


---

## Glossary: Instrumentality of State
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/instrumentality-of-state/

Bodies that are substantially financed, owned, or controlled by government — even if not a government department in the strict sense — can qualify as an instrumentality of the State for various legal purposes, including how certain DPDPA exemption provisions apply. Determining whether a particular public-sector-adjacent entity (a PSU, an autonomous statutory body) falls within this category is a fact-specific legal question we work through carefully with government and PSU clients rather than assuming either way.


---

## Glossary: Public Interest Processing
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/public-interest-processing/

The DPDPA recognises that certain government and quasi-government functions — issuing benefits, subsidies, certificates, licences, or permits — need to process personal data in ways that would be impractical to gate behind individual, itemised consent at every step. Specific Legitimate Use and exemption provisions accommodate this, but the accommodation is scoped to the specific function, not a blanket licence for any public-interest justification an organisation might assert.


---

## Glossary: Research, Archiving and Statistical Purposes Exemption
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/research-archiving-statistical-exemption/

The DPDPA exempts processing necessary for research, archiving, or statistical purposes from certain of its provisions, recognising that these activities often require handling personal data at a scale or in a manner that a fully individuated consent model would make impractical. This exemption is conditional on standards the Central Government may prescribe, and is generally understood to require appropriate safeguards — it is not an unconditional carve-out for any activity an organisation chooses to label as "research."


---

## Glossary: Employment Purposes
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/employment-purposes/

The DPDPA recognises processing for purposes related to employment — payroll, background verification, performance management, provision of any service or benefit sought by an employee — as a Legitimate Use not requiring the standard consent flow, subject to safeguarding the Data Principal's interests. This does not mean employee data is unregulated; notice, security safeguards, and rights fulfilment obligations still apply, but the consent-collection mechanic itself is not the primary gate for this category of processing.


---

## Glossary: Data Fiduciary Obligations
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-fiduciary-obligations/

Data Fiduciary Obligations is the collective term for the core duties the Act imposes: giving proper notice, obtaining and honouring valid consent (or a valid Legitimate Use basis), implementing reasonable security safeguards, ensuring the accuracy and completeness of personal data used to make decisions or shared onward, retaining data no longer than necessary, notifying breaches, and honouring Data Principal rights requests. Nearly every service we offer maps to one or more of these obligations directly.


---

## Glossary: Data Fiduciary Accuracy Obligation
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-accuracy-obligation/

Where personal data is likely to be used to make a decision affecting a Data Principal, or is to be disclosed to another Data Fiduciary, the Act requires the Data Fiduciary to ensure the completeness, accuracy and consistency of that data. This obligation is easy to overlook because it doesn't map neatly to a single UI flow the way consent does — it requires operational discipline around data quality, particularly for data feeding automated decisions or shared with partners.


---

## Glossary: Breach Notification Timeline
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/breach-notification-timeline/

The draft DPDP Rules propose that the Data Protection Board be notified of a breach without delay, with a more complete report following within a defined window thereafter, and that affected Data Principals be informed in clear and plain language describing the nature and likely consequences of the breach. Because the initial notification window is tight, organisations need a pre-built classification and escalation process rather than one improvised during an actual incident — exactly the gap our Breach Response & Notification Readiness service closes.


---

## Glossary: Notice Language Requirements
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/notice-language-requirements/

To make notice genuinely accessible across India's linguistic diversity, the Act requires that notice be available in English or any of the languages specified in the Eighth Schedule to the Constitution, at the Data Principal's option. In practice this means organisations with a broad national user base need a localisation strategy for notice content, not just a single English-language privacy policy translated informally after the fact.


---

## Glossary: Draft DPDP Rules, 2025
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/draft-dpdp-rules-2025/

The DPDPA 2023 is a framework statute — many of its operative details (breach notification timelines, consent manager registration criteria, DPIA specifics, cross-border transfer notification mechanics) are left to be prescribed through Rules. The draft DPDP Rules, 2025 fill in much of that operative detail. Because Rules can be amended more readily than the Act itself, staying current on Rules developments — not just the Act's text — is essential to accurate compliance advice, and something we track actively for every client engagement.


---

## Glossary: Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY)
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/meity/

The Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) is the Central Government ministry responsible for administering the DPDPA — issuing Rules under the Act, notifying Significant Data Fiduciaries and cross-border transfer restrictions, and constituting the Data Protection Board. MeitY's notifications and Rules are where much of the Act's practical detail actually lives, which is why monitoring the Ministry's publications is a standing part of how we keep client advice current.


---

## Glossary: Consent Fatigue
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/consent-fatigue/

Consent fatigue describes what happens when Data Principals are asked for consent so often, or so vaguely, that they stop engaging meaningfully with the request — clicking through without reading, or reflexively declining everything. It undermines the DPDPA's "informed" consent standard even where the mechanics are technically compliant. The Consent Manager ecosystem and profile-based, asset-level purpose models are both partial industry responses to this problem, and it's a design consideration we build into every Consent Management Advisory engagement, not just a UX nice-to-have.


---

## Glossary: Purpose Taxonomy
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/purpose-taxonomy/

A purpose taxonomy is the agreed, organisation-wide list of distinct processing purposes — service delivery, KYC verification, marketing, fraud prevention, and so on — used consistently everywhere a purpose needs to be referenced: notice copy, consent UI, Data Processing Agreements, and structured registers like the DPDR and CDJR. Without a shared taxonomy, different teams invent slightly different purpose labels for the same underlying activity, which quietly breaks the traceability those registers are built to provide.


---

## Glossary: Data Fiduciary Contact Publication
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/contact-publication-requirement/

Beyond simply designating a contact person, the Act expects that contact information be genuinely accessible to Data Principals — typically published prominently within a privacy notice or on a website — rather than technically existing but practically undiscoverable. Auditing whether required disclosures are actually easy for an ordinary user to find, not just technically present somewhere on a site, is a standard check in every Gap Assessment we run.


---

## Glossary: Independent Data Auditor
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/independent-data-auditor/

Significant Data Fiduciaries must engage an independent data auditor to conduct their periodic data audit — a role that must be genuinely independent of the organisation being audited, distinguishing it from an internal compliance team's self-review. Our Compliance Audit & Certification Support service prepares organisations to pass this audit with organised, defensible evidence; it operates alongside, not in place of, the independent auditor's own statutory role.


---

## Glossary: Data Protection by Design
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-protection-by-design/

Data protection by design means privacy requirements — purpose specification, data minimisation, security safeguards, rights-fulfilment hooks — are considered during initial product architecture and design, not bolted on just before launch or, worse, after a gap is discovered in production. It is the hallmark of organisations at our Level 5 (Optimised) DPDP Readiness tier, and a discipline we work to instil through embedded review checkpoints rather than a one-off audit.


---

## Glossary: Rights Fulfilment SLA
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/rights-fulfilment-sla/

A Rights Fulfilment SLA is the target response time an organisation commits to internally for handling a given category of Data Principal request — access, correction, erasure, grievance, or nomination — calibrated to the emerging expectations under the draft Rules and to operational reality. Defining and consistently meeting these SLAs, with an audit trail proving it, is a core deliverable of our Data Principal Rights Fulfillment Setup service.


---

## Glossary: Consent Withdrawal Propagation
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/consent-withdrawal-propagation/

When a Data Principal withdraws consent, the obligation to stop processing does not stop at the system that captured the original consent — it must propagate to every downstream system and Data Processor that subsequently received that data for the withdrawn purpose. Designing this propagation path, so a withdrawal recorded in one place actually takes effect everywhere it needs to, is a common technical gap in organisations with fragmented data architecture, and a specific focus of our Consent Management Advisory and Central Consent Engine implementation work.


---

## Glossary: Data Sharing Disclosure
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/data-sharing-disclosure/

As part of the right to access, a Data Fiduciary must be able to tell a Data Principal not just what data it holds about them, but which Data Processors and other Data Fiduciaries that data has been shared with, and what was shared. This requires maintaining an accurate, queryable record of data-sharing relationships — which is exactly why vendor and Data Processor due diligence work feeds directly into rights-fulfilment readiness, not just contract risk management.


---

## Glossary: Harm
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/harm-dpdpa/

The Act defines harm broadly to include bodily harm, distortion or theft of identity, harassment, prevention of lawful employment, psychological manipulation, financial loss, restriction on free movement, discriminatory treatment, and other significant adverse effects. This broad definition underlies why obligations like reasonable security safeguards and breach notification are triggered by the risk of harm generally, not a narrow, fixed list of qualifying injuries.


---

## Glossary: Consent Manager Registration
URL: https://www.readydpdp.com/glossary/consent-manager-registration/

To operate as a Consent Manager, an entity must register with the Data Protection Board and satisfy technical, operational, financial and accountability criteria specified under the Act and Rules — including interoperability standards so a Data Principal's consent record is portable and reliable across the Data Fiduciaries it connects to. This registration bar is intended to ensure Consent Managers are trustworthy intermediaries, not simply another data broker under a different name.


---
